label: ECM
rationale: obs[S4]: ECM 1205, recorded live June 1980 at the Theater am Kornmarkt, Bregenz, Austria; original release 1 September 1981 (S4, S2, S5, S6). The year field carries the recording year, 1980, per the ECM module's recording-year rule; the release year 1981 is documented separately (see personnel_record notes). obs[S3]: one continuous concert set by the four Ornette Coleman alumni — Don Cherry (trumpet, piano on 'Mopti'), Dewey Redman (tenor saxophone, musette on 'Broken Shadows'), Charlie Haden (double bass) and Ed Blackwell (drums) — playing six pieces: three Coleman tunes ('Happy House', 'New Dream', 'Broken Shadows') plus one each by Cherry ('Mopti'), Redman ('Rushour') and Haden ('Playing'). obs[S1]: AllMusic styles the album Avant-Garde Jazz, Free Jazz and Post-Bop (a stray 'Pop' tag rides along — recorded here as a classification artifact, not evidence), and Scott Yanow's 3-star review calls it 'Recommended, as are Old and New Dreams' other three releases' while allowing that 'Cherry's chops were not quite in peak form anymore'. obs[S1]/[S5]/[S9]/[S10]: producer Manfred Eicher, engineer Martin Wieland (one of Eicher's trusted engineers — S9); design Barbara Wojirsch, cover photograph Luigi Ghirri, liner photograph Roberto Masotti, and a cover quote from novelist Peter Handke whose publishers (Suhrkamp; Farrar, Straus & Giroux) hold the printed copyright (S5, S9). obs[S2]: reception splits by era and outlet — the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide (1985) gives 5/5, the Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings (9th ed., 2008) 3/4, AllMusic 3/5; JazzTimes's Ethan Iverson names Playing one of the group's two essential LPs ('the picks are the studio Black Saint, Old and New Dreams, and the live ECM, Playing') and would keep 'Happy House' above any other single Old and New Dreams track (S9); Tyran Grillo calls it 'the place to start' with the group (S10 — an ECM-appreciation blog; enthusiasm noted as source bias). inf: no source in this pass documents placement on a major published canon list; the case rests on the personnel-lineage continuity documented in continuity_case, not on canon-list placement.

continuity_case: This is the Ornette Coleman diaspora, and the lineage argument IS the case: the quartet is the 1960s free-jazz lineage the canon is built on, reconvened. Cherry and Haden were the trumpet-and-bass half of the Coleman quartet that made the canon's own The Shape of Jazz to Come, Change of the Century and Free Jazz; Blackwell succeeded Billy Higgins in that band and anchored its mid-1960s period; Redman joined Coleman for the Science Fiction era and then carried that chair into Keith Jarrett's American Quartet alongside Haden (S9). Half the record's book is Coleman's, including 'Happy House' and 'Broken Shadows' — tunes the band had learned for Science Fiction — so the record literally plays the canon's own source material forward, in that band's harmolodic, melodically explicit language extended rather than replaced: Iverson hears 'pure diatonic melody' from Redman against 'the blues' from Cherry, halftime rhythm-section feels under the horn solos, and joyous collective improvisation — 1960s free-jazz practice alive in 1980 (S9). The would-the-case-stand-without-the-label test answers yes, and more plainly: on Impulse! or Black Saint — where the group's 1976 studio debut sits — this would read as a Coleman-alumni reunion date of the first rank, and nothing in the continuity argument depends on Eicher's production. What ECM genuinely contributes is legibility: per this module's own reading of the label's free-jazz edge, these players' music was never more clearly recorded than here — the house sound is the bridge, not the substance.
overlap_risk: free-jazz — the Ornette-diaspora seam. The ECM gate owns this record by module rule (the label's free-jazz edge is 'yours, not the free-jazz style's'), but the free-jazz specialist's continuity language would claim the same personnel and repertoire from the other side, and the canon already holds the Coleman source records (The Shape of Jazz to Come, Change of the Century, Free Jazz — all archived). Modal overlap is weak: no late-modal material. Dispatch-level dedup for this candidate already returned clean.
scope_flag: ECM gate — recorded June 1980, released 1 September 1981: inside the module's 1969–1985 window (extended from 1979 on 2026-09-24) and the overall 1945–1985 eligibility window the candidate already passed, but a 1980s arrival, which leans scope_call/contested. Boundary it sits on: the record reaches the 1960s lineage forward through personnel and repertoire, not through formal innovation — the only genuinely 1980s things about it are the date and the production. Strongest case against: a Coleman-alumni repertory date, however accomplished, extends a tradition rather than advancing it; AllMusic's middling 3/5 and its note that Cherry was past peak form temper the merit case; and this module's standing warning applies — the ECM presentation flatters its material, so the label must not carry the argument. Case for: the four musicians are the tradition in question, the book is the canon's own material carried forward, and both the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide (5/5) and JazzTimes treat the date as the group's essential live document.

personnel.name: Don Cherry
personnel.notes: Plays pocket trumpet (S2, S10); AllMusic and Discogs print the credit as trumpet (S1, S5). Also credited with piano at album level (S1, S2, S4, S5), documented specifically on 'Mopti' (S3 session note 'Don Cherry (p) on b', i.e. the Mopti track; corroborated S9 'memorable piano vamp' and S10 'the infectious pianism from the composer'); coverage of the piano credit beyond 'Mopti' is not documented. AllMusic also carries a vocals credit with unspecified coverage (S1).

personnel.name: Dewey Redman
personnel.notes: Also plays musette — the credit Wikipedia links to the suona, a Chinese double-reed horn — documented on 'Broken Shadows' (S3 session note 'Dewey Redman (mus) on e', i.e. the Broken Shadows track; corroborated S10 'Redman's musette also unfurls' on Broken Shadows); album-level musette credit in S1, S2, S4, S5. Musette is not in the instrument taxonomy, so it is recorded here as a documented double rather than a primary instrument. Composed 'Rushour' (title printed as one word by every source).

personnel.name: Charlie Haden
personnel.notes: Bass credit printed as 'bass' (S2, S4, S10) and as 'Double Bass' (S1, S5). Composed 'Playing'; the original LP sleeve prints his dedication 'This song is dedicated to the children of the world' under the title (S5).

personnel.name: Ed Blackwell
personnel.notes: Sessionography lists only (d) for this session — no percussion doubles documented for this date, unlike other Old and New Dreams dates where Blackwell plays gong (S3).

personnel_record.notes: Live recording, single concert, dated June 1980 by every source but to no specific day (S2, S3, S4, S5, S10); recording_dates and session_date therefore carry ISO month precision (1980-06). MusicBrainz dates the original 12″ vinyl release '1980-06' and Apple's releaseDate serializes the same month as 1980-06-01 — neither is a documented concert day. The sessionography's June 6, 1980 entry is a DIFFERENT Old and New Dreams concert (Garten der Nationalgalerie, Berlin, private recording) — do not conflate it with this session (S3). Released 1 September 1981 on ECM (S4); Wikipedia and Discogs place the original LP in 1981 (S2, S5); MusicBrainz also holds a 1981 German 12″ promo and a 2001 US CD reissue (S6); Apple shows ℗ 1981 ECM Records GmbH (S7). Year field = 1980, the recording year, per the ECM module's rule; the id follows the dispatch's release-year filename, which deviates from the module's recording-year id convention (Conference of the Birds, recorded 1972/released 1973, carries id -1972) — flagged for the staging step. Venue: recorded live at the Theater am Kornmarkt, Bregenz — printed by ECM as 'Theater am Kornmarkt, Bregenz' (S4), by the sessionography as 'Theater am Kornmarkt, Bregenz, Austria' (S3), on the LP sleeve credit line as 'Concert Recording, June 1980, Theater am Kornmarkt, Bregenz. Austria' (S5), and by AllMusic as 'Theater Am Kornmarkt, Bregenz, Austria' (S1); Iverson places the June 1980 recording 'in performance at Theater am Kornmarkt in Bregenz, Austria' (S9) and Grillo as 'Recorded live, June 1980, Theater am Kornmarkt, Bregenz (Austria)' (S10). Wikipedia's infobox renders an English translation, 'The Cornmarket Theater' (S2) — same venue, German name authoritative. Place identity resolved via German Wikipedia: the Vorarlberger Landestheater's Stammhaus (permanent home) is the Theater am Kornmarkt, the 1838–40 Kornhaus rebuilt as a theater house in 1951–55; Dehio Vorarlberg 1983, cited there, documents the building address as Kornmarktstraße 1. Nominatim on that documented address and the building's Wikidata P625 (Q2533524, via de.wikipedia 'Theater am Kornmarkt' → Vorarlberger Landestheater) agree within ~6 metres, so the pin is street-grade obs; the Wikidata item's postal address (Seestraße 2) is the company's mailing address and was not used for the pin. Production: producer Manfred Eicher (S1, S2, S5, S9, S10); engineer Martin Wieland (S1, S5, S9, S10). The LP sleeve additionally credits 'Engineered at Tonstudio Bauer' (S5) — ECM's Ludwigsburg studio, where the concert tape was engineered; the session itself is the Bregenz concert, so Tonstudio Bauer is recorded here in notes rather than as a recording site. Design Barbara Wojirsch; cover photograph Luigi Ghirri; liner photograph Roberto Masotti (S1, S5, S9). No source in this pass names a liner-notes author — unknown, recorded as a gap. Track durations: ECM's current catalogue, Wikipedia and the sessionography agree (11:07/7:56/9:04/7:01/9:58/9:46, total 54:52 — S2, S3, S4); the original LP sleeve timings run slightly different (11:20/7:40/9:20/7:04/9:47/9:51 — S5) — transfer/pressing variance, not alternate takes. Sides follow the original single LP: A1–A3, B1–B3 (S3, S5). Original pressings: Germany ECM 1205 / 2301 205; US ECM-1-1205; Japan ECM 1205 / Trio PAP-25517 (S5, S6). Style-classification conflicts preserved as content: AllMusic lists Avant-Garde Jazz, Free Jazz, Post-Bop plus a stray Pop tag (S1); Discogs styles it Contemporary Jazz (S5); Wikipedia gives genre Jazz only (S2). style_primary free-jazz follows AllMusic's Free Jazz/Avant-Garde Jazz classification and this module's placement of Old and New Dreams in the label's free-jazz edge; post-bop is recorded as a genuine secondary style from AllMusic.

scope_check.boundary_note: Recorded in June 1980 and released in 1981, it is inside the 1945–1985 window, but it sits at the doubly cautious 1980–85 tail and at the opened ECM/free-jazz gates: the key question is whether it extends the 1960s lineage or mainly documents a repertory reunion.

ballot.case_for: The album has exceptional session gravity and lineage: Don Cherry, Charlie Haden, Ed Blackwell, and Dewey Redman collectively embody the Coleman diaspora behind canonical records including The Shape of Jazz to Come, Free Jazz, and Science Fiction, while half the set carries Coleman repertoire forward (S3, S9). Ethan Iverson identifies it as one of Old and New Dreams' two essential LPs and emphasizes its diatonic melody, blues grounding, swinging rhythm section, and joyous collective improvisation; the accessible live recording therefore offers a strong discovery bridge into free jazz rather than an abrasive outlier (S9).
ballot.case_against: The dossier documents no major published canon-list placement, while reception is mixed: Penguin gives it 3/4, AllMusic 3/5, and Scott Yanow notes that Cherry was no longer at his peak, despite the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide's 5/5 (S1, S2). A skeptical listener may hear a well-recorded, nostalgic Coleman-alumni repertory date rather than a defining statement or forward-moving 1980s development, especially since the canon already contains the foundational Coleman records; ECM's clarity may improve legibility without changing that underlying limitation.
ballot.disagreement: The references agree that the album is inside the window and merits consideration, but they differ on whether the decisive classification is contested quality or a scope call: Reference 1 emphasizes the unusually strong lineage and session-gravity case while retaining contested, whereas Reference 2 treats the 1980s/ECM/free-jazz continuity boundary as primary and assigns scope_call.
ballot.recommendation: John should consider it as a strong lineage-and-discovery candidate, while deciding whether this live repertory document extends the canon's tradition enough to cross its 1980s ECM/free-jazz boundary.
